Title: The gut microbiome and incident atherosclerotic cardiovascular events: Prospective analyses in three Swedish cohorts
Authors: Pertiwi, K.; Hammar, U.; Dekkers, K.; Coward, E.; Kambur, O.; Baldanzi, G.; Delgado-Velandia, M.; Sayols-Baixeras, S.; Yuan, S.; Persson, P.; Gabrielsson, D.; Miari, M.; Volpiano, C. G.; Meric, G.; Jönsson, D.; Engström, G.; Smith, J. G.; Michaëlsson, K.; Melander, O.; Ärnlöv, J.; Knight, R.; Hofmann, R.; Niiranen, T. J.; Havulinna, A. S.; Salomaa, V.; Hveem, K.; Ohlsson, C.; Orho-Melander, M.; Larsson, S. C.; Fall, T.
Abstract: BackgroundVariation in the gut microbiome composition has been associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in case-control designs. We aimed to investigate associations with incident ASCVD events applying a prospective design to reduce the impact of reverse causality.  MethodsWe assessed associations between gut microbiome features measured by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and incident total ASCVD, ischemic heart disease (IHD) and ischemic stroke, including fatal and non-fatal events as defined by registry follow-up in 17,216 participants from three Swedish population-based cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS). Results from Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for demographic, and lifestyle factors, medication, and prevalent diabetes were combined across cohorts using a fixed-effect meta-analysis accounting for multiple testing. Associations were tested for replication in HUNT and FINRISK.  ResultsDuring a median of 6-8 y follow-up, 769 incident ASCVD events occurred. Species diversity was inversely associated with ASCVD and IHD, with a hazard ratio for IHD of 0.86 per SD increase in species richness (95% CI: 0.79-0.95). Sixty-eight common species (i.e., present in [≥]30% individuals) were associated with incident IHD after adjusting for sex and birth country, but only eight remained in fully adjusted models, including Ruminococcus_B gnavus. Among others, inverse associations were observed for SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 from Christensenellales, an order in which butyrate production has been reported. Streptococcus mutans and Limosilactobacillus fermentum, oral-associated species previously associated with coronary atherosclerosis, were associated with a higher risk of incident IHD, which remained after adjustment for dental health. Replication analysis in the HUNT study supported the finding for S. mutans. No associations were observed with ischemic stroke.  ConclusionsGut species diversity and specific species abundance were associated with incident IHD, providing evidence supporting a protective role of two Christensenellales species and an adverse role of oral species and R. gnavus in the development of IHD.

Title: Gut microbiome associations with incident cardiovascular disease in Nordic populations
Authors: Wolford, B. N.; Larsson, S. C.; Nethander, M.; Lawenius, L.; Pertiwi, K.; Kambur, O.; Coward, E.; Gynnild, M. N. N.; Giskeodegard, G. F.; Asvold, B. O.; Grahnemo, L.; Erkorkmaz, B. A.; Engström, G.; Smith, J. G.; Salomaa, V.; Dekkers, K.; Ärnlöv, J.; Havulinna, A. S.; Volpiano, C. G.; Meric, G.; Niiranen, T. J.; Orho-Melander, M.; Fall, T.; Ohlsson, C.; Hveem, K.
Abstract: BackgroundThe gut microbiome is an emerging risk factor for cardiovascular disease. However, there is a lack of large-scale metagenomic studies with replication that identify gut microbial features associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD).  MethodsWe tested for gut microbiome associations with CVD using metagenomes from stool samples in a discovery-replication framework across four large prospective Nordic cohorts with 635 incident CVD in 11,604 participants in the discovery cohort and 2,309 incident CVD in 20,965 participants combined across three replication cohorts.  ResultsHigher Shannon diversity index and species richness were consistently associated with a lower risk of incident CVD. In addition, the relative abundance of nine species and eleven bacterial functional modules showed reproducible associations with incident CVD in the discovery cohort and in a meta-analysis of the three replication cohorts. We identified a female-specific gut microbiota-related pathway involving the prevalent oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, enriched among denture users, thus serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health. Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal effect of denture use on increased relative abundance of Rothia mucilaginosa_A. This pathway was linked to increased CVD risk through altered gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating imidazole propionate levels, and increased levels of systemic inflammation biomarkers. The second pathway involved both -diversity metrics and the remaining eight species, all of which were strongly associated with multiple markers of metabolic syndrome and with bacterial pathways related to purine metabolism, microbial stress responses, altered redox balance, ascorbic acid degradation, and branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis.  ConclusionsThese findings demonstrate that gut microbiota diversity, specific taxa, and functional pathways provide new insights into the underlying biology of CVD. Furthermore, these findings suggest that the link between poor oral health and cardiovascular disease may, at least partly, operate through altered gut microbiota.

Title: Aging, Structural, and Neighborhood-Environmental Correlates of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Factor Burden Across U.S. Census Tracts
Authors: Batobara, A.; Alfaraidhy, M.; Tanriover, B.; Liu, Y.; Damluji, A. A.; Vest, A. R.; Lim, C.
Abstract: BackgroundThe American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023. Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling. It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions.  MethodsWe built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020. In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging x environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning. The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcomes BRFSS source; a second added them. Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates.  ResultsAgreement with NHANES was modest. Burden clustered spatially (Morans I = 0.657) and highest in the South. Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing. Each percentage-point increase in adults [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts. LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile. Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses. The primary models residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both.  ConclusionsCKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South. LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts. These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment. C_LIO_LIEach 1-percentage-point higher share of adults aged [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (crude prevalence, not age-standardized). Title: Optimizing dosing strategies for children with leprosy: A weight-banded dosing approach
Authors: van Dyk, J.; Masini, T.; Lambert, S. M.; Darlong, J.; Deps, P. D.; Nobre, M. L.; van Brakel, W.; Hill, B.; Timalsina, A. B.; Mane, S. S.; Malik, P.; Lal, V.; Wasmann, R. E.
Abstract: BackgroundDosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations.  MethodologyA pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to 10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80-125% of adult area under the concentration-time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility.  ResultsProposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10-14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25-39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6-24.9 kg.  ConclusionsA harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed.  Author SummaryLeprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available.  In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care.  This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.

Title: A framework for guiding integrated disease control measures through multipathogen surveillance
Authors: Bents, S. J.; Ante-Testard, P. A.; Hu, H.; Rerolle, F.; Kamau, E.; Njenga, S. M.; Kanyi, H.; Kihoro, R. W.; Emisiko, H.; Rahman, M.; Ashraf, S.; Parvez, S. M.; Ali, S.; Rahman, M. Z.; Miah, M. R.; Shakil, M.; Shoab, A. K.; Haque, R.; Goodhew, E. B.; Coleman, C.; Grembi, J. A.; Mertens, A. N.; Stewart, C. P.; Priest, J. W.; Lammie, P. J.; Lin, A.; Benjamin-Chung, J.; Ercumen, A.; Pickering, A. J.; Null, C.; Colford, J. M.; Luby, S. P.; Lo, N. C.; Arnold, B. F.
Abstract: Global health programs have traditionally focused on single diseases. There is potential for synergy through integrated intervention delivery, particularly in areas with overlapping geographic disease burden, but there is limited methodology developed to guide integration. Here, we propose a framework to translate multipathogen surveillance data into summary indices that can guide integrated program delivery to target multiple pathogens at once. We considered several measures of diversity to quantify multipathogen infection or undervaccination across three large-scale surveys: subregions in Bangladesh (90 clusters, n = 7,187) and Kenya (89 clusters, n = 9,077), and a national survey in Cambodia (100 clusters, n = 2,150). We found that strategies guided by a measure of diversity, Raos quadratic index, consistently identified more efficient integrated strategies than other multipathogen indices across a range of intervention combinations. We then identified case studies in each setting that used immunization as the backbone for integration and found that incorporating information from co-occurring pathogens led to only modest reductions in efficiency for vaccine-preventable diseases, while affording potentially large gains for other pathogens. Compared with a strategy that prioritized a single vaccine-preventable disease, prioritization using a multipathogen index required targeting 4% (95% CI: 0-12%) fewer spatial clusters in Bangladesh to target four additional pathogens, 10% fewer clusters in Kenya (95% CI: 3-17%), and 11% (95% CI: 5-22%) fewer clusters in Cambodia to reach 80% of all potential intervention beneficiaries across diseases. In all settings, we observed geographic clustering of multiple pathogens, with moderate to high spatial autocorrelation in Bangladesh (Morans I = 0.58), Kenya (I = 0.56), and Cambodia (I = 0.26), indicating potential for more efficient, spatially concentrated integrated interventions. We also found that a multipathogen index was significantly associated with a multidimensional poverty index in Bangladesh (Spearmans {rho} = 0.25), Kenya ({rho} = 0.51), and Cambodia ({rho} = 0.59), suggesting that multipathogen-guided strategies may effectively target impoverished populations with the highest public health need. The framework provides a systematic approach to guide integrated program delivery, offering potential for greater efficiency in disease control.

Title: An integrative eco-entomovirological study of Culicoides species associated with Oropouche virus in Colombia
Authors: Mantilla, J. S.; Garcia-Guzman, S.; Salcedo-Amortegui, C. J.; Calvo-Tapiero, E. P.; Cardozo, D. A.; Castellanos, J. E.
Abstract: BackgroundOropouche virus (OROV) causes recurrent outbreaks in South America, including Colombia. Although Culicoides paraensis is the principal recognized urban vector, the potential involvement of other Culicoides species remains incompletely understood. In Colombia, studies combining viral detection, host-feeding behavior, and ecological suitability are scarce.  MethodologyWe investigated Culicoides communities in urban and peri-urban environments of Puerto Carreno, Vichada, during two seasonal transitions. Species identification combined morphology and COI DNA barcoding, and blood-meal sources were identified using vertebrate molecular markers. OROV RNA was assessed by RT- qPCR targeting the L and S genomic segments, and maximum likelihood prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals were calculated accounting for unequal pool sizes, including a conservative estimate based on concordant detection of both targets. Selected positive samples underwent multiplex amplicon sequencing fragments from all three OROV genomic segments (L, M, and S) using Oxford Nanopore Technology, followed by consensus reconstruction and phylogenetic analysis. Ecological suitability models were compared with reported OROV case distributions.  Principal FindingsWe collected 1,639 specimens representing 11 taxa, eight supported by COI barcoding. C. insignis accounted for more than 70% of captures and was the only taxon collected in urban settings. OROV RNA was detected in C. insignis, C. pusillus, and C. ignacioi. In C. insignis, concordant detection of the L and S molecular targets yielded an estimated prevalence of 3.61 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 0.94-9.60). Nanopore sequencing recovered OROV-derived fragments spanning up to 656 nt across the L, M, and S genomic segments. Shorter fragments supported molecular identification, while phylogenetic analysis of a 656-nt M-segment region recovered from C. insignis and C. pusillus placed both sequences within a group containing viruses associated with the recent South American outbreak, although partial genomic coverage prevent formal lineage assignment. Blood-meal analyses identified feeding on humans, horses, and pigs in C. insignis; humans and horses in C. pusillus; and horses in C. ignacioi. Ecological models identified distinct environmental associations among species, and predicted suitability for overlapping portions of regions reporting OROV cases. Administrative-scale concordance was heterogeneous.  ConclusionsThe integration of molecular, host-feeding, and ecological evidence highlights C. insignis, C. pusillus, and C. ignacioi as species of epidemiological interest in the context of OROV circulation in Colombia. These findings expand current knowledge of OROV-associated Culicoides diversity and provide a basis for targeted entomological surveillance and experimental studies to clarify their potential roles in virus transmission.  Author SummaryOropouche virus (OROV) causes recurrent outbreaks in South America, including Colombia. Although Culicoides paraensis is the principal recognized urban vector, the possible involvement of other biting midge species remains poorly understood. We investigated Culicoides communities in urban and peri-urban environments of Puerto Carreno, eastern Colombia, combining species identification, blood-meal analysis, viral RNA detection, sequencing, and ecological modeling. OROV RNA was detected by RT-qPCR in C. insignis, C. pusillus, and C. ignacioi. Genetic sequencing confirmed the presence of OROV-derived sequences. Partial viral M segment sequences grouped with references associated with recent South American outbreaks, although they did not allow formal lineage assignment. C. insignis was the most abundant species, with repeated viral detections and evidence of feeding humans and domestic animals. Ecological models showed distinct environmental associations among species and variable overlap with regions reporting human cases. Together, these findings highlight the potential epidemiological relevance of multiple Culicoides species and provide a basis for targeted surveillance and experimental studies to clarify their roles in OROV transmission.

Title: Digital cytometry of immune cell types from dried blood microsamples
Authors: Ferry, Q. R.; Rajakumar, T.; Zeeck, M.; Chong-Morrison, V.; von Schrenck, T.; Ahmadi-Simab, K.; Steinkraus, B. R.
Abstract: Enumeration of circulating immune cells is an established clinical practice implemented across a plethora of indications. While flow cytometry is the gold standard for this task, cellular deconvolution algorithms provide a robust computational alternative using molecular data. These digital cytometry pipelines typically rely on millilitre-scale venous blood samples. Here, we evaluated the potential of capillary blood microsampling as a patient-centric and minimally invasive approach for the digital cytometry of major lymphocyte populations (T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells; TBNK). In a cohort of 200 participants, we compared RNA sequencing based deconvolution performance between matched PAXgene-stabilised venous blood and Mitra capillary blood microsamples. While venous transcriptomes enabled highly accurate TBNK estimation, patient-matched capillary microsamples exhibited a significant reduction in deconvolution accuracy. Computational adaptations, including the integration of capillary-specific single-cell reference profiles, yielded only limited improvements. Instead, our analyses revealed that the performance deficit was primarily driven by the decreased transcriptome complexity of the capillary microsample libraries. This study highlights the critical role of transcript diversity for cellular deconvolution and reveals the current pre-analytical challenges that must be overcome to harness transcriptomics based digital cytometry using dried blood microsamples.

Title: Population-level indirect effects of HPV vaccination in high-income settings: a Bayesian modelling study
Authors: Wang, R.; Jit, M.
Abstract: BackgroundHuman papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination provides direct protection to vaccinated individuals, but also indirectly protects unvaccinated individuals through reduced HPV transmission. Mechanistic transmission models that predict the magnitude of such effects have been crucial to informing vaccination strategies. However, nearly two decades of post-vaccination experience in high-income countries now allow us to empirically characterise how population-level indirect effects vary with vaccine coverage, time since vaccine introduction, and age.  MethodsWe synthesised studies reporting HPV16/18 prevalence before and after vaccine introduction in high-income settings between 2007 and 2025. Indirect effects were estimated as the observed reduction in HPV16/18 prevalence after accounting for expected direct vaccine protection. We used a Bayesian hierarchical model to examine associations with vaccine coverage, time since vaccine introduction, and age at effect assessment across routine, catch-up, and non-targeted vaccination groups. XGBoost was used as a complementary, non-parametric approach.  FindingsData from 11 high-income settings were included. Indirect effects increased during the first five to eight years after vaccine introduction and then remained relatively stable. Indirect effects generally decreased with increasing vaccine coverage. Patterns with age differed across vaccination groups. In the routine group, indirect effects increased during adolescence and remained positive at older observed ages. In the catch-up group, indirect effects decreased with age and approached zero or became negative after approximately age 25 years. XGBoost identified similar non-linear patterns.  InterpretationIndirect protection against HPV16/18 develops gradually after vaccine introduction and varies with vaccine coverage, age, and vaccination group. This empirical approach can complement transmission models by using real-world evidence to characterise population-level indirect protection. However, making predictions outside the populations and ranges represented in the data should be done cautiously.  FundingThis study received no specific funding.  Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed for studies published up to Oct 26, 2026. The search terms were ("HPV vaccin" [All Fields] OR "human papillomavirus vaccin" [All Fields]) AND ("herd immunity" [All Fields] OR "herd effect" [All Fields] OR "indirect effect" [All Fields] OR "indirect protection" [All Fields] OR "herd protection" [All Fields]). We included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, and modelling studies that assessed the indirect effects of HPV vaccination on HPV infection or HPV-related outcomes. We excluded studies that focused exclusively on direct vaccine protection or economic evaluations that included herd immunity without separately estimating or reporting indirect effects.  We identified 301 articles, of which 77 met the inclusion criteria: 52 observational studies, 22 modelling studies, and three systematic reviews or meta-analyses. From those studies, two systematic reviews by Drolet and colleagues (2015 and 2019) synthesised evidence from 14 high-income countries and provided evidence of herd protection following vaccine introduction. A meta-analysis of results from 16 transmission dynamic models by Brisson and colleagues (2016) projected substantial herd effects under different vaccination coverage levels. More recently, an observational study by Meglic and colleagues (2026) used nationwide registry data from Sweden and found age-varying herd effects, with lower incidence of high-grade cervical lesions among unvaccinated women in cohorts exposed to school-based vaccination. Despite growing real-world evidence from high-income countries over nearly two decades, few studies have examined how indirect protection varies with vaccination coverage, time since programme introduction, and age across settings.  Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to synthesise real-world HPV16/18 prevalence data from 11 high-income settings to estimate the indirect effects of HPV vaccination over the period 2007-2025. Our findings show that indirect protection generally increases during the first several years after vaccine introduction before stabilising, with different patterns across age groups and vaccination programmes.  Implications of all the available evidenceAs countries work towards cervical cancer elimination, understanding the indirect protection provided by HPV vaccination is important for assessing its broader population-level impact. This multi-country evidence complements transmission-dynamic models and provides an empirical basis for evaluating the long-term effects of HPV vaccination programmes.

Title: Nirsevimab effectiveness against RSV hospitalizations in children 8-23 months at risk of severe RSV
Authors: Simeone, R. M.; Newhams, M. M.; Payne, A. B.; Orzel-Lockwood, A. O.; Calixte, J.; Halasa, N.; Kamidani, S.; Crandall, H.; Irby, K.; Maddux, A. B.; Zerr, D.; Guzman-Cottrill, J.; Schuster, J.; Chiotos, K.; Kong, M.; Staat, M. A.; Hume, J.; Stockwell, M. S.; Cameron, M.; Hogan, A. H.; Chauhan, J.; Biggs, A.; Levy, E. R.; Bhumbra, S.; Walker, T. C.; Marupudi, N. K.; Prahl, M. K.; Michelson, K. N.; Martin, L.; Brandford, T.; Randolph, A.; Campbell, A. P.; Overcoming RSV Network investigators,
Abstract: ImportanceRespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of hospitalization in high-risk young children during their second RSV season. Nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody against RSV, is recommended for some children who are at increased risk for severe RSV and entering their second RSV season to prevent severe RSV disease. Because of limited eligibility criteria for second season nirsevimab, estimating its effectiveness is challenging.  ObjectiveWe evaluated nirsevimab effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalizations among young children eligible to receive nirsevimab during their second RSV season.  DesignThis retrospective case control study with a test-negative design was conducted during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 RSV seasons.  SettingEnrollment was in 26 hospitals across 24 U.S. states.  ParticipantsChildren eligible for nirsevimab during their second RSV season (as recommended in August 2023) were included. Nirsevimab-eligible children 8-23 months old hospitalized with respiratory symptoms were enrolled. Case-patients tested positive for RSV; control-patients tested negative for RSV.  ExposuresReceipt of nirsevimab before or during the childs second RSV season and at least 7 days before symptom onset.  Outcomes and measuresRSV-associated hospitalization. We estimated nirsevimab effectiveness using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, month and year of hospitalization, census region, and sex comparing the odds of second season nirsevimab receipt among case- and control-patients.  ResultsOne hundred six case-patients and 125 control-patients were analyzed. Distributions of age, sex, race and ethnicity, and region were similar in case- and control-patients. Most case- and control-patients were eligible for nirsevimab because of chronic lung disease of prematurity (84.0% and 69.6%, respectively). Overall, 21 (19.8%) of case-patients and 53 (42.4%) of control-patients received nirsevimab. Adjusted nirsevimab effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalizations was 78.1% (95% CI, 55.2%-89.3%); the median interval from nirsevimab receipt to symptom onset was 66.5 days (IQR = 30-96 days). Effectiveness was estimated to be higher if nirsevimab was received 8-59 days before symptom onset (88.5%, 95% CI, 63.4%-96.4%).  ConclusionsThis analysis provides real-world estimates of substantial nirsevimab effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalizations for high-risk U.S. children in their second RSV season These data support recommendations for nirsevimab as a preventive strategy in this population.  Key PointsO_LIQuestion: What is the effectiveness of nirsevimab against RSV-associated hospitalizations among children 8-23 months old who are at risk for severe disease and in their second RSV season? C_LIO_LIFindings: In this case-control study of hospitalizations for acute respiratory illness among high-risk children in their second RSV season, receipt of nirsevimab was associated with an estimated 78% reduction in risk of RSV-associated hospitalizations. C_LIO_LIMeaning: Nirsevimab provided substantial protection against RSV-associated hospitalizations in children at high risk of severe RSV during their second RSV season. C_LI

Title: Emergent Heterogeneity in Compartmental Disease Models
Authors: Roswell, M.; Aghaeeyan, A.; Goel, T.; Beckett, S. J.; Weitz, J. S.; Dushoff, J.
Abstract: Heterogeneity in infectious disease spread reshapes the risk and severity of outbreaks. This heterogeneity can arise from intrinsic individual-level differences in susceptibility, contact patterns, and infectious durations. Heterogeneity can also emerge from disease dynamics in a canonically homogeneous population, due to the fact that individuals randomly become infected at different times, recover after different intervals, and have access to different numbers of susceptible individuals. Here, we explore the mechanisms generating emergent heterogeneity by analyzing secondary case distributions within the SIR model. We show numerically and prove analytically that the variation in secondary cases, calculated over the course of the epidemic, does not change with R0. This is in contrast to the increasing variation in secondary cases in the linearized SIR model, often used to study heterogeneity at the beginning of an outbreak. When we consider "forward cohorts" of individuals infected at the same time, between-cohort variation increases as R0 increases, while within-cohort variation decreases. We show that these effects balance exactly, leading to the invariance of the variation in secondary cases with respect to R0. These results demonstrate the importance of considering emergent, as well as intrinsic, variation between individuals and of considering heterogeneity of transmission spread over the whole epidemic cycle, including substantive dynamical effects that appear even in the initial outbreak phase.

Title: Wastewater sequence data reveal national and cross-border virus transmission dynamics
Authors: Odor, G.; Endler, L.; Amman, F.; Bergthaler, A.
Abstract: Spatial epidemic models estimate disease transmission counts between populations using human mobility data, but location-to-location transmission is rarely observed directly. To address this gap, we develop mutation-counting methods to infer transmission structure from viral genetic variation measured in wastewater. In epidemic simulations with known transmission networks, our primary estimator robustly recovers spatial structure under realistic mutation-detection limits. Applied to spatiotemporal SARS-CoV-2 wastewater data from Austria, the method reveals strong seasonal reorganization, with inferred transmission becoming more geographically localized in winter and more dispersed in summer. We further identify locations with systematically higher or lower connectivity than expected from commuting, with temporal changes coinciding with regional restrictions, reopening and tourism. We then test whether such inference remains possible across national borders, recovering coherent spatial structure and temporal variation in connectivity between Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. These results establish wastewater sequence data as a promising complement to mobility data for monitoring spatial transmission and detecting changes in epidemic spread associated with seasonality and interventions.

Title: Chatbot as an intervention on physical activity: A systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression
Authors: Fu, L.; Song, D.; Bai, Y.
Abstract: BackgroundChatbots offer scalable, accessible, and personalized support for physical activity (PA). This review synthesized evidence on their efficacy and examined potential moderators.  MethodsEleven databases were searched for English-language published through January 27, 2026. Eligibility was assessed using the PICOS framework. Data extraction was guided by research questions, mERA checklist, and PRISMA 2020. Risk of bias was evaluated using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and the NIH Quality Assessment Tool. Meta-analyses reported Hedges g. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots, Eggers regression, and trim-and-fill analyses. Potential moderators were examined through subgroup analyses and meta-regression.  ResultsA total of 12,481 records were identified, of which 43 studies were included in the systematic review and 27 in the meta-analysis. Most studies included in the meta-analysis had some risk-of-bias concerns (16/27). Chatbot interventions produced a significant small-to-moderate post-intervention effect on PA (g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.19, 0.44]; n = 24), whereas the follow-up effect was small and non-significant (g = 0.11, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.22]; n = 4). Effects varied across PA outcomes (g = 0.08-0.44), and several subgroup differences helped explain the significant heterogeneity. For daily steps, significant subgroup differences were observed by clinical status, while intervention duration (QM = 6.09, p = 0.048) and clinical status (QM = 5.69, p = 0.017) were significant moderators.  ConclusionsChatbot interventions showed small-to-moderate post-intervention effects but limited follow-up effects. Few significant moderators were identified, underscoring the need for more rigorous RCTs.

Title: ASSESSMENT OF KNOWLEDGE AND DISPOSAL PRACTICES OF SPENT AND BROKEN ENERGY-SAVING BULBS AMONG HOUSEHOLDS IN MTENDERE COMPOUND LUSAKA ZAMBIA
Authors: MASELECHI, M.; Zyambo, C.; BANDA, J. L.
Abstract: The widespread adoption of energy-saving bulbs like light-emitting diodes and compact fluorescent lamps in Zambia has raised significant environmental and public health issues because some of these bulbs contain dangerous materials like mercury. This study sought to evaluate households understanding and disposal practices of used and damaged energy-saving bulbs in Lusaka, Zambias Mtendere Compound. A cross-sectional design was used, with structured questionnaires distributed to a randomly chosen sample of households. The research showed that, although most participants were aware of the energy efficiency advantages of these bulbs, they had little understanding of their possible health risks and safe disposal procedures. The majority of households reported throwing away broken and used bulbs with their regular household trash, while only a small percentage followed the suggested disposal procedures. Environmental contamination and heightened health risks are exacerbated by a lack of awareness and inadequate municipal waste management systems for hazardous household waste. The research advocates for improved public education initiatives, the creation of specific collection sites for dangerous waste, and the formulation of explicit national regulations and policies for the handling of discarded and damaged energy-saving bulbs. In rapidly urbanizing areas like Mtendere, tackling these issues is essential for protecting public health and advancing environmental sustainability.

Title: Visible Immigration Enforcement Arrests and Mental Health Among Hispanic Adults in the United States
Authors: Aslim, E.; Tekin, D.; Venkataramani, A.
Abstract: Visible immigration enforcement in community settings can create fear and distress that spill beyond the communities directly affected. In this paper we explore the relationship between state-level community-based U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest rates and mental health outcomes among Hispanic and non-Hispanic adults in the United States. We explore this question for two periods, 2023-2024 and 2025, over which visible immigration enforcement moved from a localized to a national phenomenon. In 2023-2024, poor mental health rises as local ICE arrest rates increase. Each additional non-prison arrest per 10,000 non-citizens at the state-level is associated with 0.15 additional poor mental health days per month among Hispanic adults, and with a 0.9 percentage point higher likelihood of reporting any poor mental health days, a 2.2 percent increase relative to the mean, driven mainly by female and lower-educated Hispanic adults. The relationship is null for non-Hispanic adults. By contrast, within-state deviations in ICE arrests are no longer correlated with mental health beyond the national trend in 2025. We posit that this may because ICE activity was more frequent and more synchronized and mental health deteriorated nationally relative in 2025 relative 2023-2024, potentially making local ICE activity less salient or impacts of such activity harder to detect.

Title: Antibiotic prescribing and resistance beyond hospital surveillance networks in India
Authors: Kaur, J.; Madaan, V.; Sharma, R.; Agarwal, Z.; Gudi, N.; Bisen, T.; Gupte, S.; Mutreja, A.; Doegar, N.; Singh, H.; Agarwal, G.; Sethi, T.
Abstract: Hospital-based networks provide much of the antimicrobial resistance surveillance evidence in India, but community-facing data on both prescribing and resistance remain limited. We analysed 2.78 million prescription-validated antibiotic records and 155,764 microbiology samples from Tata 1mg, a digital healthcare platform, during 2023-2025. We assessed prescribing composition and resistance trends, and explored ecological prescribing-resistance associations using merged monthly series. Access antibiotics accounted for 28.7% of records, compared with 47.0% for Watch and 11.9% for Not Recommended antibiotics. Across 25 eligible states and union territories, Access shares ranged from 16.1% to 38.0%. Urine comprised 93.9% of samples. Among urinary Escherichia coli isolates, resistance was 4.9% to nitrofurantoin and amikacin, compared with 53.6% to ceftriaxone and 57.0% to ciprofloxacin. Exploratory prescribing-resistance associations varied by organism and antibiotic. These findings identify stewardship priorities within a digitally mediated care pathway and illustrate the complementary value of routinely collected pharmacy and laboratory data for surveillance beyond hospital-centred networks. but community-facing data on both prescribing and resistance remain limited. Title: Impact of wildfire-related fine particulate matter on tuberculosis notifications in Brazil: a nationwide panel study, 2003-2023
Authors: Pham, T. M.; Mendonca, T.; Zhang, Y.; Mallia, D.; Croda, J.; Cohen, T.; Andrews, J. R.; Requia, W.; Walter, K. S.
Abstract: Wildfire activity is intensifying with climate and land-use change, but its consequences for chronic infectious diseases remain poorly understood. We linked monthly tuberculosis notifications to wildfire-related fine particulate matter (PM2.5) across 5,544 Brazilian municipalities (notifications 2005-2023; exposure 2003-2023), using a fixed-effects distributed-lag panel design that accounts for meteorology, diagnostic coverage, seasonality, and state-level trends. Fourteen additional high-exposure days (PM2.5 >25 {micro}g/m3) in a month were associated with an average increase of 2.7% [95% CI: 0.9-4.5%] in tuberculosis notifications in each of the following 24 months, peaking 11 months (IQR: 11-12) after exposure. Wildfire-related PM2.5 exposure accounted for 2.0% [0.7-3.2%] of notifications in exposed municipality-months, with the largest attributable fractions in Pantanal (12.3%, 95% CI: 8.7-15.7%) and Amazonia (6.4%, 95% CI: 5.2-7.7%). These results suggest that wildfire-related PM2.5 has a delayed effect on tuberculosis, extending health consequences of wildfire smoke beyond acute respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes and identifying a potential window for exposure-informed surveillance.

Title: Upper respiratory microbiome and host immune signatures associated with SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and illness in a human challenge model
Authors: Hurst, J. H.; Wanchai, V.; Shi, P.; Nookaew, I.; Swain-Lenz, D.; Rowlette, L.-L.; Cleaton, S.; Arnold, J.; Kim, S. Y.; Hite, C.; Kay, K. L.; Catchpole, A.; Kalinova, M.; Killingley, B.; Mann, A.; Wagstaffe, H. R.; Chiu, C.; Kelly, M. S.
Abstract: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. Baseline nasal microbiome composition differed modestly by subsequent infection status, with lower relative abundances of Corynebacterium accolens and higher abundances of Dolosigranulum pigrum and Staphylococcus aureus among participants who became infected. Integrated analyses of microbiome and host gene expression data identified coordinated networks of microbiome features and host immune modules that distinguished infected from uninfected participants, including prior to inoculation. Notably, immune modules associated with infection susceptibility were positively correlated with S. aureus abundance and negatively correlated with the abundances of common nasal commensals, Corynebacterium spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis, linking altered nasal microbiome community structure with the heightened inflammatory state associated with infection susceptibility. Symptom burden and viral load were similarly linked to distinct networks of microbiome and host gene expression features within nasal samples. Taken together, these findings highlight potential microbiome-host interactions within the nasal mucosa that may contribute to differences in respiratory viral infection outcomes.

Title: Broader functional and memory antibody responses in adult females than males in response to seasonal H3N2 vaccine virus
Authors: Park, H.-S.; Yin, A.; Parish, M. A.; Hu, J.; Zou, A.; Pandey, R.; Fenstermacher, K. Z. J.; Rothman, R. E.; Pekosz, A.; Toapanta, F. R.; Klein, S.
Abstract: Females of reproductive ages often mount greater antibody responses than males following influenza vaccination, but the breadth and depth of these differences, including antibody-dependent Fc receptor (FcR)-mediated functions have not been explored. Plasma samples were collected from male and female healthcare workers (range of 21-48y; mean of 31y) at 0, 28, and 180 days post-vaccination (DPV) during the 2022-2023 influenza vaccine season to assess antibody responses to A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria vaccine viruses. Females had greater A/H3N2, but not A/H1N1 or B/Victoria, neutralizing antibody (nAb) responses compared to males through 180 DPV, with differences being most pronounced among A/H3N2 responders ([≥]4 fold-change in nAb titers). Memory B cells isolated from female responders secreted more IgG in response to ex vivo H3 stimulation than those from males at 28 and 180 DPV. Before vaccination, female responders had greater anti-H3 IgG responses and Fc{gamma}RIIB (CD32b) antibody binding than males, with females maintaining greater responses through 180 DPV. Female responders had greater H3-specific antibody-dependent monocyte phagocytosis (ADMP) and natural killer cell (ADNK) secretion of IFN{gamma} and CCL4 prior to and after vaccination, with ADMP positively correlating with greater H3N2 neutralization through 180 DPV in females only. Among responders, the durability of ADMP, ADNK, and nAb in females as compared to males defined the sex differences in influenza-vaccine induced immunity. The greater Fc{gamma}R-binding antibodies prior to vaccination in females might improve the durability of both neutralizing and non-neutralizing antibody responses to diverse vaccines, including next generation influenza vaccines.

Title: Validation of gender identity and sexual behavior stigma measures among transgender women in the United States: Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses
Authors: Lo Hog Tian, J. M.; Atkins, K.; Murray, S. M.; Glick, J. L.; Lucas, I. L.; Valentine-Graves, M.; Winter, S.; Caldwell, J. A.; Sanchez, T.; Baral, S. D.; Wiginton, J. M.
Abstract: Introduction Transgender women experience stigma related to both gender identity and sexual behavior, yet robust measurement tools remain limited. This study evaluated the factor structure and external construct validity of the Measures of Attributional Stigma for gender identity (MAS-GI) and sexual behavior (MAS-SB) among transgender women in the United States. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional data from the Transgender Womens Internet Survey and Testing (TWIST) platform collected from 2023-2025 (N=2,901). Participants completed parallel 14-item stigma measures attributed separately to gender identity and sexual behavior. The sample was split into exploratory factor analysis (EFA; n=1,951; 2023-2024) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; n=950; 2024-2025) samples. External construct validity was evaluated via associations with depression symptoms, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social capital, transgender identity pride, and healthcare utilization. Results EFA identified three MAS-GI factors (family stigma, anticipated healthcare stigma, and enacted social stigma) and two MAS-SB factors (global healthcare stigma and social/institutional stigma). CFA confirmed both structures with good to excellent model fit. All stigma dimensions were positively associated with depression and PTSD. Anticipated healthcare and enacted social stigma from the MAS-GI and both MAS-SB dimensions were negatively associated with social capital. Greater anticipated gender identity healthcare stigma associated with lower transgender identity pride. Several stigma dimensions were also positively associated with HIV/STI testing, PrEP use, and mental healthcare utilization. Conclusions The MAS-GI and MAS-SB demonstrate factorial validity and preliminary external construct validity among transgender women. These measures enable precise assessment of stigma by attribution and source and inform stigma surveillance and intervention evaluation.

Title: Stigma and unsupportive disclosure reactions are associated with elevated depressive symptom burden among adolescent mothers in Juja Sub-County, Kenya: a community-based cross-sectional study
Authors: Kariuki, T.; Kariuki, J.; Mogere, D.; Onyancha, J.; Moriasi, G.
Abstract: Girls who become pregnant during adolescence in sub-Saharan Africa carry a high burden of depressive symptoms. Kenyan studies have relied on antenatal clinic samples and have not looked at stigma, the response to pregnancy disclosure and economic circumstances in the same analysis. We assessed how these factors relate to depressive symptom burden among adolescent mothers in Juja Sub-County, Kiambu County. We surveyed 227 girls who had been pregnant or given birth at 10-19 years, drawn by stratified random sampling from a line list of 466 mapped across five wards. Trained assistants administered a structured questionnaire covering background characteristics, pregnancy and disclosure, stigma, and a seven-item depressive symptom checklist. Elevated symptom burden was set in advance at four or more endorsed items. Two logistic regression models examined factors linked to stigma (n = 199) and to elevated symptom burden (n = 184). Of those with parity data, 194 of 197 had already given birth. Most respondents were 17-19 years old (86.8%) and single (69.2%), 92.5% had no income of their own, and 47.1% had left school early. Nine in ten pregnancies (91.2%) were unplanned, and 41.4% of girls met anger, rejection or indifference when they first disclosed. Stigma was reported by 43.2%, elevated symptom burden by 27.1% and thoughts of self-harm by 16.4%. Only 27.3% had attended any support programme. Being single was the one factor associated with stigma (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 3.50; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.48-8.31). Elevated symptom burden was associated with stigma (AOR 3.21; 1.54-6.69) and with an unsupportive disclosure reaction (AOR 2.54; 1.19-5.41), and was less likely with each additional year of age (AOR 0.69; 0.49-0.96). Programme attendance showed no association (AOR 0.89; 0.41-1.94). In this peri-urban community, depressive symptoms clustered among adolescent mothers who had been stigmatised or poorly received when they disclosed their pregnancy, and stigma tracked marital status more closely than poverty. Screening with validated tools at postnatal, child-health and antenatal visits, guidance for families and partners on responding to disclosure, and community work on attitudes to unmarried motherhood deserve testing in this setting.

Title: Changes in Health Behaviors and Correlational Patterns among High School Students Across Two Longitudinal Studies
Authors: Li, S.; Ganss, E.; Gomez, C.; Lazarchak, A.; Moriarty, C.; McIntire, R.
Abstract: Purpose - This study examines whether six health behaviors remain stable among high school students across the school year and whether associations between these behaviors recur across assessments. Design/methodology/approach - As part of a school health program evaluation, a pre-post longitudinal health survey was conducted among two samples of high school students in a U.S. vocational-technical high school. Study 1 surveyed 114 students from late winter to late spring in 2024. Study 2 surveyed 177 students from autumn 2024 to late spring 2025. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests examined group-level behavioral change, and Pearson correlation networks described associations among six health behaviors: sleep, breakfast consumption, physical activity, nature exposure, social media use, and mindfulness practices. Findings - The primary analyses detected no significant group-level changes in any of the six behaviors across either study interval, suggesting relative stability within these samples. A one-time survey may provide useful information for broad school health planning, whereas repeated assessment remains necessary for evaluating longer-term patterns or program effects. Sleep and breakfast showed the most consistent positive association. Physical activity and nature exposure were positively associated at three of the four assessments. Social media was isolated from the other behaviors at the first three assessments but was negatively associated with sleep and physical activity at the final assessment. Originality - The study distinguishes stability in group-level behavior from changes in the relationships among behaviors. The findings support efficient assessment for broad educational planning. They also identify behavior pairs that can be addressed together in school health education, including sleep and breakfast, physical activity and nature exposure, and social media, sleep, and physical activity.

Title: Nonstructural Protein 1 (NS1)-based IgG FcγR competition Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) for highly specific serological profiling of previous flavivirus exposures
Authors: Ehmen, C.; Ferraz, R.; Blessmann, J.; Sopraseuth, V.; Keoviengkhone, L.; Bispo, A.; Levy, F.; Demchyshyna, I.; Papa, A.; Jelovsek, M.; Korva, M.; Matthies, L.; Ramharter, M.; Nordmann, T.; Gabriel, M.; Günther, S.; Kann, S.; von Possel, R.; Liu, Y.; Schmitz, H.; Schmidt-Chanasit, J.; Emmerich, P.; Deschermeier, C.
Abstract: Background: Due to extensive antibody cross-reactivity, serological discrimination of IgG antibodies elicited by exposure to different flaviviruses remains challenging. We aimed to develop and validate highly discriminative IgG ELISAs employing an Fc{gamma} receptor (Fc{gamma}R) capture platform and recombinant competitor molecules to suppress cross-reactive responses. Methods: IgG ELISAs targeting Dengue virus (DENV), Zika virus (ZIKV), and West Nile virus (WNV) were established using immobilized human Fc{gamma}RIIA for antibody capture and soluble, labeled nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) as antigen. To suppress flavivirus cross-reactivity, target-specific competitor molecule formulations (Specificity Enhancers (SEs)), comprising unlabeled heterologous NS1 proteins, were incorporated. ELISAs were validated using comprehensive serum panels from Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Results: Validation revealed reliable detection of seroconversion following DENV, ZIKV, and WNV infections, as well as DENV vaccination. In sera from flavivirus-endemic regions, substantial cross-reactivity was observed in the absence of SEs, predominantly in samples showing strong reactivity to the corresponding homologous antigen. Addition of SEs significantly improved specificity without compromising sensitivity in most sample panels. In complex exposure settings, analysis of differential signal modulation by individual SE components may provide insights into possible exposure histories. Notably, serological discrimination between IgG antibodies elicited by exposure to different WNV lineages could be achieved by combining lineage-homologous NS1 antigens with lineage-heterologous competitor molecules. Conclusions: The flavivirus (NS1) IgG Fc{gamma}R SE ELISA platform enables enhanced differentiation of flavivirus-specific IgG responses in epidemiologically complex settings. Its modular design allows versatile adaptation to newly emerging flaviviruses and supports high-resolution seroepidemiological investigations in One Health contexts.

Title: Perinatal suicide risk factors: A network analysis
Authors: Zivin, K.; Zhong, C.; Kahsay, E.; Johns, L.; Spring, E.; Courant, A.; Mezuk, B.
Abstract: Purpose Suicide during pregnancy or after birth (the perinatal period) represents a leading, preventable cause of United States maternal deaths. This study aimed to understand the complex relationship between perinatal status and life circumstances among perinatal suicide decedents in the United States and generate insights regarding suicide risk. Methods This cross-sectional study used decedent data from the 2003-2023 National Violent Death Reporting System suicide mortality registry (N=20,217). We applied psychometric network analysis using 18 binary life circumstances indicators representing four domains: relationships, health, socioeconomic status, and risk factors for suicide. We generated two networks for the overall sample and perinatal sample and assessed network structure, bridge centralities, and stability. Results The analytic sample included 1,297 perinatal and 18,920 non-perinatal decedents. The network of the overall sample was stable. Perinatal status did not appear at the center of the network but connected primarily with intimate partner problems. The network of the perinatal sample was modestly stable. Postpartum status was not at the center of the network but connected to depressed mood and mental health diagnoses. In both networks, depressed mood had the highest bridge betweenness, and there was a consistent link between physical health domains and socioeconomic domains. Conclusion Suicide prevention strategies targeting childbearing-aged women should incorporate factors beyond pregnancy, including physical health, intimate partner relationships, and socioeconomic challenges.

Title: Designing infection prevalence and seroprevalence surveys for learning infection dynamics
Authors: Creswell, R.; Golding, N.; Ryan, G. E.; Eales, O.; Price, D. J.; McCaw, J. M.; Shearer, F. M.
Abstract: Knowledge of the true number of infections over time is valuable for accurately predicting the future course of an epidemic and planning effective interventions, but the number of cases reported offers only a noisy underestimate of the true number of infections. Disease surveillance strategies based on assessing subsets of the population for current infection (infection prevalence surveys) or antibody presence (seroprevalence surveys) yield crucial information about the number truly infected, but are expensive. To explore impact of survey design considerations--both sample size and sampling frequency--on inference of the number of incident infections over time, we coupled agent-based simulations of respiratory virus epidemics with simulations of infection prevalence and seroprevalence surveys. While returns diminish with increased sample size, we find inference generally improved by increasing survey frequency relative to participants-per-round for any given sample size. After survey rounds reach a sufficient frequency, comparable inference performance may be achieved with either more frequent rounds or more participants per round. Rolling designs with tests conducted each day tend to outperform designs in which testing is divided into discrete rounds. We also show that misspecified assumptions about seroreversion may substantially decrease the quality of inference results.

Title: Validity and reliability of the Japanese version of the Movement Behaviour Questionnaire-Child (MBQ-C) for assessing active play, screen time, and sleep in preschool children
Authors: Komura, K.; Yamakita, M.; Kyan, A.; Inoue, S.; Nagano, M.; Takenaga, R.; Breugelmans, R.; Jego, E. H.; Trost, S. G.
Abstract: Background: Valid and feasible measures of preschoolers' 24-hour movement behaviours are needed for population-level research. We developed a Japanese version of the Movement Behaviour Questionnaire-Child (MBQ-C) and evaluated its measurement properties and practicality. Methods: After translation and cross-cultural adaptation following the COSMIN procedure, including cognitive interviews, we evaluated the questionnaire in a cross-sectional validation study of Japanese children aged 3-6 years. Concurrent validity was assessed against hip-worn accelerometry and a 7-day diary; we also examined test-retest reliability, measurement error, agreement between response formats and modes, and practicality (completion time, burden, and clarity). Analyses used Spearman correlations, intraclass correlation coefficients, the SEM, smallest detectable change (SDC), and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: Of 208 children, 170 provided valid accelerometer and diary data for the concurrent-validity analysis, and 187 completed the MBQ-C for the questionnaire-based analyses. Concurrent validity was weak for active and energetic play (Spearman {rho} = 0.12-0.26), strong for total screen time (0.78-0.85), and moderate for total sleep (0.48-0.58). Test-retest reliability was moderate to good (ICC, 0.66-0.81), and within-child variability was lowest for sleep (CV 3%) and highest for the physical activity items (21-33%). The open- and closed-ended versions showed no significant differences; paper-electronic agreement was good for screen time and sleep but poor for active play. Completion took approximately 6-9 minutes, with low reported burden. Findings were robust in sensitivity analyses. At the group level, SDC for a mean was SDCind/{surd}N: 119.8/{surd}N, 74.0/{surd}N, 112.6/{surd}N, and 92.5/{surd}N min/day for active play, energetic play, total screen time, and total sleep, respectively (N = number of children surveyed). The systematic differences between the two test-retest occasions were +15.7, +6.5, +4.0, and -5.4 min/day, respectively. Conclusions: The Japanese MBQ-C is a practical option for assessing preschoolers' active play, screen time, and sleep at the group level. By quantifying its group-level measurement error, this study provides benchmarks for interpreting group-level differences and change, supporting the use of the MBQ-C in surveillance and evaluation of programmes delivered at scale.

Title: Nicotine pouch adverts reach 12 times more young men than women: targeting and reach on Meta social media platforms in the UK
Authors: Sun, H.; Jackson, S. E.; Xiao, L.; Cox, S.; Oldham, M.; Jiang, Y.; Tattan-Birch, H. O.
Abstract: Abstract Aims To examine which demographic groups nicotine pouch advertisers chose to target on social media, and which groups Meta's algorithms actually delivered the adverts to. Design Cross-sectional analysis of advert-level data from the Meta Ad Library. Setting Meta social media platforms (including Facebook and Instagram) in the UK. Cases A sample of 642 nicotine pouch adverts identified by keyword search, shown in the 12 months up to December 2025, and a comparison sample of 1,125 general adverts. Analyses of reach were restricted to adverts with no advertiser-set gender restriction that targeted all adult ages (373 pouch adverts; 674 general). Measurements Outcomes, both extracted from the Meta Ad Library, were advertiser-set gender and age-group targeting criteria (i.e., groups eligible to be shown each advert) and estimated advert reach to each group (i.e., number of people who saw each advert). Male-to-female reach ratios (RR) within age groups, and reach ratios comparing age groups, were calculated per advert and summarised using geometric means. To assess whether patterns were pouch-specific, comparisons with general adverts were made using ratios of reach ratios (RRR). Findings Advertisers of nicotine pouches targeted a broad sample. Most adverts 81.0% (520/642) had no gender restriction, the remainder were restricted to men only. All were restricted to adults (minimum age 18 years) and most (96.9%; 622/642) had no upper age limit. Despite this, of pouch adverts eligible to be shown to all adults, adverts were more likely to reach men, particularly among younger men. Among 18-24-year-olds, pouch adverts reached around twelve times as many men as women (RR 12.5, 95% CI 10.9-14.4), compared with a slight skew towards women for general adverts (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.95), corresponding to an RRR of 15.4 (95% CI 12.3-18.8). Pouch adverts also showed a skew in reach towards younger age groups. Relative to those aged 35-44 years, reach was higher among 18-24-year-olds for nicotine pouch adverts (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.31-1.71) but much lower for general adverts (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.17-0.21), corresponding to an RRR of 7.9 (95% CI 6.6-9.5). Conclusions Nicotine pouch adverts on social media were often eligible to be shown broadly to all demographic groups but were disproportionately delivered to young men.

Title: Detection of Peanut Allergy Sensitization and Monitoring of Type 2 Memory B cells Using Recombinant Peanut Allergen Components
Authors: Reinwald, S.; Aui, P. M.; Fettes, R. L.; Deckert, K.; Hogarth, P. M.; Hew, M.; O'Hehir, R. E.; van Zelm, M. C.
Abstract: Background Peanut allergy is one of the most common causes of life-threatening food allergy, and therefore the focus of multiple clinical trials for allergen immunotherapy. Diagnosis relies on detection of allergen-specific serum IgE, which provides limited information on severity and threshold. Furthermore, objective biomarkers to predict allergic persistence and efficacy of treatment are lacking. Therefore, we aimed to incorporate recombinant peanut allergen components in a multiplex Cytometric Basophil detection assay (CytoBas) for detection of peanut sensitization, and in a memory B cell (Bmem) panel for evaluation of biomarkers of disease. Methods In 27 adult peanut-allergic patients, allergen-specific IgE levels were determined by ImmunoCAP, and component-specific IgE by ELISA. PBMC of all patients and of 15 non-sensitized controls were analyzed by flow cytometry with basophil markers and six fluorochrome-conjugated allergen component tetramers for CytoBas, while circulating Bmem were studied including fluorescent tetramers for Ara h 1, Ara h 2 and Ara h 3. Results CytoBas demonstrated similar-to-improved diagnostic performance compared to IgE ELISAs for Ara h -1, -2, -3, -6, -8 allergens (ROCs AUC 0.79-1.0 versus 0.78-0.9). Ara h 2 discriminated all patients from controls, while combined Ara h 1, 3 and 6 (excluding major allergen Ara h 2) elicited 78-81% sensitivity with 100% specificity. Peanut-allergic patients showed expansion of the pathogenic Type 2 Bmem subset within Ara h 1-, 2- and 3-specific cells, and the Ara h 1+ and Ara h 3+ Bmem contained expanded IgG4+ and IgG1 subsets. Conclusions Peanut CytoBas displays similar to superior diagnostic accuracy to component-specific IgE serology, enabling efficient evaluation of multiple allergen components in a single test tube. Peanut-allergic individuals show increased frequencies of allergen-specific type 2 Bmem, which could be longitudinally evaluated to monitor the natural course of disease or allergen immunotherapy.

Title: Modeling spontaneous hepatitis C virus clearance by age, sex, IFNL4 genotype, and infection history: Implications for simulations of elimination and vaccine trials
Authors: Gandhi, K. R.; Mao, S.; Tatara, E.; Ozik, J.; Boodram, B.; Cotler, S. J.; Major, M.; Gutfraind, A.; Dahari, H.
Abstract: Background and Aims: The probability of hepatitis C virus (HCV) clearance is mediated by an interaction between numerous factors. However, variation in spontaneous HCV clearance was previously modeled using relatively simple approaches with fixed probabilities by sex. Here, we developed a literature-informed clearance algorithm that considers age, sex, interferon lambda 4 (IFNL4) genotype, and infection history to model the probability of HCV clearance in vulnerable populations, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), and in controlled human infection (CHI) models for future HCV vaccines. Methods: We modeled HCV clearance probabilities for three infection-history pathways: first infection, reinfection after spontaneous clearance, and reinfection after direct-acting antiviral (DAA) cure. Logistic and cumulative-hazard equations assigned person-specific clearance probabilities in the first two pathways. The post-DAA pathway used fixed clearance probabilities. We tested the algorithm using HepCEP (Hepatitis C Elimination in PWID), an agent-based simulator. Results: First-infection clearance probabilities ranged from 0.13 to 0.51 across eight age, sex, and IFNL4 genotype subgroups. Clearance probabilities for reinfection after spontaneous clearance ranged from 0.20 to 0.80 at literature point estimates. Across 100 runs, the mean assigned clearance probabilities were 0.27 for first infections and 0.52 for reinfections after spontaneous clearance, compared with literature inputs of 0.26 and 0.52, respectively. Probabilities varied across subgroups and runs. Conclusion: Simulations reproduced the algorithm's intended clearance heterogeneity and uncertainty by age, sex, IFNL4 genotype, and infection history, which may support models of HCV elimination in vulnerable populations and CHI model development for future HCV vaccines.

Title: Improving UK Biobank algorithms for Parkinson's disease ascertainment using drug claims
Authors: Kimmerling, V.; Jaber, E.; Proust-Lima, C.; TRUONG, T.; Elbaz, A.
Abstract: Background: Accurate ascertainment of Parkinson's disease (PD) is a major challenge in large-scale epidemiological studies. The UK Biobank (UKB) is widely used for PD research, but ascertainment based on hospital and death records may result in misclassification and delayed PD diagnoses. Objectives: We compared different strategies for ascertaining PD in the UKB, and examined their impact on incidence and associations with risk factors and mortality. Methods: We compared PD ascertained through hospital and death records (ADO-PD) to two approaches that rely on primary care data available for ~45% of participants: diagnoses from general practitioner consultations (Clinical-PD); a novel drug-based algorithm (Drug-PD). We compared incidence, age at diagnosis, and associations with sex, walking speed, and mortality across all algorithms. Results: ADO-PD identified ~20% fewer prevalent and incident cases than Drug-PD over 15y of follow-up, and estimated age at diagnosis to be 4.2y (median) later than age at anti-PD drugs initiation. ADO-PD identified never treated participants or with other causes of parkinsonism as PD patients. While Drug-PD yielded incidence rates consistent with UK reference rates, ADO-PD underestimated incidence by 36% compared to reference rates. Associations with sex, walking speed, and mortality were significantly different for ADO-PD compared to Drug-PD. Clinical-PD and Drug-PD yielded similar findings, although Clinical-PD included patients with other causes of parkinsonism. Conclusions: We draw attention to methodological issues regarding PD ascertainment in the UKB and their consequences. These results can help inform strategies for PD ascertainment by combining multiple data sources, thereby improving the validity of epidemiological analyses.

Title: Childhood and adolescent cancer diagnosis, treatment, and hospitalizations during the COVID-19 pandemic in Quebec, Canada, a population-based study
Authors: Mullen, C.; Barr, R.; Coltin, H.; Strumpf, E.; El-Zein, M.; Franco, E.; Malagon, T.
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted healthcare delivery globally. In Quebec, Canada, measures were introduced to prioritize pediatric oncology care. Using administrative data, we estimated pandemic-related changes in cancer diagnoses, treatments, and length of hospital stay among individuals aged 0-19 in Quebec (2015-2023). Interrupted time series analyses using autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models assessed immediate and sustained changes in monthly age-standardized rates of diagnoses, treatments (chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy-related encounters), positron emission tomography scans, and hospital admissions. Separate ARIMA models fitted to pre-pandemic monthly counts generated counterfactual forecasts to estimate the cumulative differences between observed and expected diagnoses and treatments over 3, 12, and 46 months of the pandemic. Generalized linear mixed models assessed changes in length of stay between the pre- and post-pandemic periods and whether these changes differed by patient characteristics. We identified 2,570 patients: 1,475 diagnosed through February 2020 and 1,095 from March 2020 onward. We found no evidence of immediate or sustained changes in monthly incidence rates. Cumulative diagnoses and treatments remained within expected levels across periods, although estimates were imprecise. For diagnoses, the 3-, 12-, and 46-month cumulative differences were -1 (95% uncertainty interval [UI] -17 to 15), 24 (95% UI, -9 to 57), and 2 (95% UI, -94 to 96), respectively. Changes in length of hospital stay varied across subgroups, although their clinical significance remains uncertain. Pediatric cancer diagnosis and treatment activity was largely maintained across Quebec throughout the pandemic, consistent with the objectives of provincial and institutional measures to preserve pediatric oncology services.

Title: Positive association of abdominal subcutaneous fat with cardiometabolic risk in thin, young Indians: A window on the developmental trajectory of adiposity-based chronic disease (ABCD)
Authors: Wagh, R. S.; Bawdekar, R. U.; Alenaini, W.; Fall, C. H.; Thomas, E. L.; Bell, J. D.; Prasad, R. B.; Khare, S. P.; Yajnik, C. S.
Abstract: Background: The thin-fat Indian phenotype defined as lower lean mass and higher adiposity compared to Europeans, is present at birth and progresses throughout the lifecourse. While this increases cardiometabolic risk from a young age, there is scant information on the individual contributions of subcutaneous and visceral abdominal fat to cardiometabolic risk in young Indians. Western population-based studies link visceral adiposity (VAT) rather than abdominal subcutaneous adiposity (ASAT) to cardiometabolic disease. However, some South Asian Indian population-based studies have reported an association of ASAT with cardiometabolic risk. Whether this association persists in young South Asian populations remains unclear. We investigated associations of ASAT and VAT with cardiometabolic risk markers in young rural Indian adults. Methods: We quantified ASAT and VAT using MRI at 18-years of age in 310 men and 280 women from the Pune Maternal Nutrition Study birth cohort. Sex-specific multiple regression models examined cross-sectional (18-years) and prospective (24-years) associations of ASAT and VAT with a range of cardiometabolic risk markers, and also with change in risk (delta) between two time points; adjusting for obesity indices and birth size. Findings: In regression models, ASAT was strongly associated with more adverse cardiometabolic profiles (higher glucose, lipids, blood pressure, leptin, CRP, leukocyte count, and lower adiponectin and Matsuda Index), consistently showing higher effect estimates than VAT in both sexes (beta ranging from 0.45 to 0.88 in ASAT vs 0.13 to 0.18 in VAT, p<0.05). ASAT at 18-years remained significantly associated with levels of cardiometabolic risk factors at 24-years, and also with the change in their level from 18-years. These associations were independent of obesity and birth size. Interpretation: Our findings suggest a possible role for ASAT in increasing cardiometabolic risk in young Indians, raising a possibility of novel adipocyte pathobiology. Despite an observational design, consistency of associations across time (18- and 24-years) and temporality are compatible with a causal hypothesis.

Title: Broader functional and memory antibody responses in adult females than males in response to seasonal H3N2 vaccine virus
Authors: Park, H.-S.; Yin, A.; Parish, M. A.; Hu, J.; Zou, A.; Pandey, R.; Fenstermacher, K. Z. J.; Rothman, R. E.; Pekosz, A.; Toapanta, F. R.; Klein, S. L.
Abstract: Females of reproductive ages often mount greater antibody responses than males following influenza vaccination, but the breadth and depth of these differences, including antibody-dependent Fc receptor (FcR)-mediated functions have not been explored. Plasma samples were collected from male and female healthcare workers (range of 21-48y; mean of 31y) at 0, 28, and 180 days post-vaccination (DPV) during the 2022-2023 influenza vaccine season to assess antibody responses to A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria vaccine viruses. Females had greater A/H3N2, but not A/H1N1 or B/Victoria, neutralizing antibody (nAb) responses compared to males through 180 DPV, with differences being most pronounced among A/H3N2 responders ([≥]4 fold-change in nAb titers). Memory B cells isolated from female responders secreted more IgG in response to ex vivo H3 stimulation than those from males at 28 and 180 DPV. Before vaccination, female responders had greater anti-H3 IgG responses and Fc{gamma}RIIB (CD32b) antibody binding than males, with females maintaining greater responses through 180 DPV. Female responders had greater H3-specific antibody-dependent monocyte phagocytosis (ADMP) and natural killer cell (ADNK) secretion of IFN{gamma} and CCL4 prior to and after vaccination, with ADMP positively correlating with greater H3N2 neutralization through 180 DPV in females only. Among responders, the durability of ADMP, ADNK, and nAb in females as compared to males defined the sex differences in influenza-vaccine induced immunity. The greater Fc{gamma}R-binding antibodies prior to vaccination in females might improve the durability of both neutralizing and non-neutralizing antibody responses to diverse vaccines, including next generation influenza vaccines.
